name: Smart Went Crazy
label: Dischord
lede: Five DC kids, an electric cello, a Laurie Anderson cover and a 73-minute second album that the people who made it were glad to walk away from.

eras.title: A band for school holidays
eras.text: Smart Went Crazy began as something three friends did when they were home from school. Dischord describes it as a low-key partnership between Chad Clark, Abram Goodrich and Hilary Soldati, and the first record came out on the band's own tiny label.

years.h: Smart Went Crazy starts, playing only on school breaks
years.p: [[Chad Clark|f3f09e99-e31c-4aa2-99e4-0b4e59e72f87]] on guitar and voice, Abram Goodrich on bass, Hilary Soldati on cello. According to Dischord, the trio played together only during school breaks.

years.h: Smart Went Crazy's Cubbyhole EP, on their own CozyDisc
years.p: Smart Went Crazy's debut EP goes out on CozyDisc, the band's own imprint, before any label came calling.

eras.title: Five people and a cello
eras.text: After graduation the part-time trio became a full band, added a second guitar and a drummer, and landed on Dischord. What set Smart Went Crazy apart in a guitar town was Hilary Soldati's electric cello, sawing and droning where a lead guitar would usually go.

years.h: Smart Went Crazy become a quintet
years.p: After graduation, [[Jeff Boswell|6c40b2b3-cabb-40a2-85d6-ceab52159cd1]] joins Smart Went Crazy on guitar and Tony Dennison on drums, with Hilary Soldati's electric cello in the middle of everything.
years.xp:
Dischord's history says the band expanded only after its members graduated. The cello was the signature: the Ernest Jenning reissue notes single out Hilary Soldati's electric cello as the band's most distinctive element.

Soldati also played organ on Now We're Even, and sang. Chad Clark wrote and sang most of the songs and would go on to produce the band's records himself.

years.p: Smart Went Crazy's first full-length, eighteen songs recorded in summer 1995 with Tony Dennison on drums. Titles run from Best and Final Offer to Garden Variety Hate Song.

years.h: Smart Went Crazy tour the US three times
years.p: Dischord counts three US tours behind Now We're Even. Out of that road time came the band's first line-up change.

years.h: Tony Dennison out, Devin Ocampo in
years.p: [[Devin Ocampo|10bc183b-b6a8-4769-9e7a-0637d0f8a7a8]] takes over Smart Went Crazy's drums from Tony Dennison. He plays on everything that came after, and later proves just as good a guitarist.

years.h: Live at the Hurricane, Kansas City, August 12, 1996
yt: Live at the Hurricane, Kansas City, August 12, 1996

eras.title: The long record, the short goodbye
eras.text: Con Art was huge on purpose: 18 songs and 73 minutes, meant as a double album, produced by Chad Clark and the band at Inner Ear. It sounded almost nothing like the DC punk around it, and by the time it came out the band already suspected it was the last one.

years.p: Smart Went Crazy's second album, recorded at Inner Ear Studios and produced by Chad Clark and the band. Eighteen tracks and 73 minutes, from Black Kites to the two-part DC Will Do That To You.
years.xp:
Treble's retrospective hears it as the record where Smart Went Crazy broke from DC punk tradition: cello, space and long quiet stretches instead of volume. It was conceived as a double LP, the format Ernest Jenning finally gave it twenty years later.

Chad Clark has said the band could feel during the sessions that this would be the last one.

years.h: Smart Went Crazy cover Laurie Anderson on Con Art
years.p: Con Art includes Let X=X, a [[Laurie Anderson|86809b51-cbe2-45f1-804a-e66eed635dea]] song, played by a Dischord band. Not the cover anyone expected.

years.h: Smart Went Crazy break up over clashing personalities
years.p: Less than a year after Con Art, Smart Went Crazy were done. Wikipedia puts it down to internal tensions.
years.xp:
Chad Clark told Treble the band broke up because of intense personalities and conflicting ideas among five emotionally driven people. He called the end of it a relief.

Dischord's own history is shorter: the band dissolved in 1998, shortly after Con Art came out.

years.h: Devin Ocampo picks up a guitar
years.p: After Smart Went Crazy, Devin Ocampo switches to guitar and vocals and goes on to [[Faraquet|e866e006-4c80-4753-b53f-1bc5d88ccddd]], then [[Medications|c545a7bf-c8d7-4368-8009-22e19d8911ce]], where Jeff Boswell briefly played bass.

eras.title: A cult record grows up
eras.text: Smart Went Crazy stayed broken up, but Con Art kept gaining ground: on critics' lists, in other musicians' record collections, and finally on the vinyl it was meant for. Chad Clark built a second act with Beauty Pill and as a producer, through two heart operations.

years.h: Chad Clark and Abram Goodrich start Beauty Pill
years.p: Chad Clark and Abram Goodrich start [[Beauty Pill|976b28a1-dd68-4c43-ba08-ba15b58963b2]] after Smart Went Crazy dissolves, with Devin Ocampo drumming. Clark also becomes a busy producer and engineer for [[The Dismemberment Plan|1131e5da-dfdf-46c9-b6ff-b7ac552c2a3c]], [[Q and Not U|a934e33f-b3cb-47dd-9638-f7f1f25fe162]], [[Black Eyes|50d90400-e7ea-4465-92a5-404605e51ee7]] and [[Mary Timony|d9c8dc3c-15b8-40d5-8153-ae9214aeef55]].

years.h: Chad Clark survives emergency heart surgery
years.p: Chad Clark developed viral cardiomyopathy in fall 2007 and had emergency open-heart surgery in February 2008, Wikipedia reports. In spring 2022 he needed an emergency heart transplant.

years.cap: Con Art, reissued as the double LP it was meant to be
years.h: Twenty years on, Con Art gets its double LP
years.p: Ernest Jenning announces a remastered, vinyl-only double LP of Smart Went Crazy's Con Art from the source tapes: 500 copies on clear vinyl, redesigned by Henry Owings of Chunklet. Dischord distributes it as EJRC143.
years.xp: The reissue notes call it an underground classic whose stature increased with time, and point to Pitchfork putting it on its list of the best albums of the 1990s. Chad Clark has joked to Treble that he's made more money from the record being an influence on other musicians than from its royalties.
